stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD HITS FRESH 2002 HIGH AT 5.35% EVEN AS SEPTEMBER PAYROLLS COME IN AT JUST 29,000
stories.body: The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield jumped as much as 7 bps intraday to 5.349% — its highest level since April 2002 — before settling near 5.31%, up 3 bps on the day, despite a September jobs report that showed only 29,000 nonfarm payrolls added and unemployment rising to 4.2%. The 2-year yield actually eased to 4.82%, so the move was concentrated at the long end of the curve.
stories.explain: A weak jobs print normally pulls yields down because it raises the odds of Fed easing, but long-end yields are priced off two separate components: the expected path of short rates and the term premium investors demand for holding duration risk. Here, the term-premium piece dominated — soft growth data combined with French fiscal turmoil (see below) and persistent deficit concerns pushed investors to demand more compensation for owning 10-year paper, even as the front end, which tracks Fed-policy expectations more directly, rallied slightly. That's why the curve can steepen on bad growth news instead of flattening the way textbook intuition suggests.

stories.headline: S&P 500 CLIMBS TO 7,774, NASDAQ-100 TO 31,076 AS AI-TRADE NAMES SHRUG OFF BOND WEAKNESS
stories.body: The S&P 500 rose 0.66% to 7,774 and the Nasdaq-100 added 0.87% to 31,076, with SpaceX jumping more than 7% and Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Tesla all posting gains of roughly 1-2%. The Nasdaq Composite closed at a record 27,477.31, up 1.05%.
stories.explain: Equities decoupling from rising yields usually signals that investors are reading the same data — a soft labor market — as disinflationary and supportive of eventual Fed cuts, even if the long end of the curve is pricing a separate fiscal-risk story. Mega-cap AI names with strong balance sheets and limited near-term refinancing needs are less sensitive to higher discount rates than rate-sensitive sectors, which is part of why the rally concentrated in that cohort rather than broadening out.

stories.headline: DOLLAR INDEX TOPS 102.5, AN 18-MONTH HIGH, AS FRENCH BOND TURMOIL DRIVES HAVEN FLOWS INTO THE GREENBACK
stories.body: The DXY touched 102.54 intraday before settling near 102.27, up 0.33% on the day and its strongest level since April 2025, as a French fiscal shock hit European sovereign debt and pushed the British pound and euro lower against the dollar. The index is now up 4.24% over the past 12 months.
stories.explain: When a major sovereign borrower's fiscal credibility comes into question, global capital doesn't wait to see how it resolves — it rotates toward the deepest, most liquid safe asset available, which is still U.S. Treasuries and the dollar, even with America's own yields near 24-year highs. That's the mechanism behind a stronger dollar coexisting with weaker U.S. jobs data: the dollar's move here is being driven by a relative flight from France, not by a verdict on U.S. fundamentals.

stories.headline: OIL MARKETS SPLIT: BRENT HOLDS ABOVE $102 AND MURBAN HITS $110 WHILE WTI SLIPS TOWARD $91 ON RISING MIDEAST SUPPLY
stories.body: Brent crude held above $102/bbl and UAE's Murban grade spiked to $110, even as WTI crude eased roughly 0.5% to near $91 as markets weighed rising Middle East crude exports against lingering Strait of Hormuz security risk. Gold stalled just below $4,150/oz, down about 0.06%, as rising Treasury yields offset its usual haven bid.
stories.explain: Brent and Murban are seaborne grades priced directly off Gulf shipping risk, so they carry a geopolitical risk premium that WTI — a landlocked U.S. benchmark less exposed to Hormuz transit risk — doesn't fully share, which is why the same headlines can push one grade up and leave another roughly flat. Gold's muted reaction despite real geopolitical stress shows the yield effect dominating: gold pays no coupon, so a 24-year-high 10-year yield raises its opportunity cost even while it would normally catch a safe-haven bid from an oil-security scare.

stories.headline: PTC CORP SOARS 33% AS SCHNEIDER ELECTRIC AGREES TO $22 BILLION ALL-CASH ACQUISITION
stories.body: PTC Corp shares jumped 33% after Schneider Electric announced an all-cash deal to acquire the company for $22 billion, the day's biggest single-stock mover. Moderna (+6.95%) and Visa (+2.53%) also posted notable advances in an otherwise AI-led tape.
stories.explain: An all-cash deal removes acquisition-financing risk for the target's shareholders and typically prices in close to the full takeout premium immediately, which is why PTC's stock jumped straight to a level reflecting the deal price rather than drifting toward it — the market is pricing a high probability the deal closes as announced rather than any ongoing standalone-business risk.

stories.headline: ST. JOHN'S GUARD DONNIE FREEMAN OUT FOR THE SEASON AFTER ACHILLES SURGERY
stories.body: Rising junior guard Donnie Freeman suffered a non-contact Achilles injury in a workout and underwent surgery, ruling him out for the entire 2026-27 season before it tips off. Coach Rick Pitino confirmed the injury directly: "Donnie had a non-contact injury in a workout and will miss the season." The loss is a significant blow to St. John's depth heading into Big East play, which begins in November.

stories.headline: KARL-ANTHONY TOWNS SAYS KNICKS EXTENSION 'DOESN'T LOOK GOOD' BEFORE SEASON OPENER
stories.body: Knicks center Karl-Anthony Towns, eligible for a four-year, $276 million extension, said the prospects of a new deal getting done before the regular season begins aren't looking good. The comments come as New York opened its preseason schedule against Philadelphia, with the Sixers now fielding LeBron James and Jaylen Brown alongside Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey, and VJ Edgecombe.

stories.headline: CHIEFS EDGE RAIDERS 30-27 TO END LAS VEGAS'S PERFECT START AS PANTHERS UPSET LIONS ON SUNDAY NIGHT
stories.body: Kansas City improved to 4-0 by beating the previously unbeaten Raiders 30-27, while Carolina upset Detroit 32-26 in the Week 4 Sunday Night Football finale. Elsewhere, the Giants' Jameis Winston threw three touchdowns and Deonte Banks returned a pick-six 98 yards to beat Arizona 36-24, and Chicago routed the Jets 23-12 behind a 492-157 total-yardage margin — the Bears' best such margin since 1979.

stories.headline: OHIO STATE'S JEREMIAH SMITH SETS PROGRAM RECORDS AS ALABAMA AND MISSOURI DELIVER WEEK 5'S BIGGEST ROAD WINS
stories.body: Ohio State receiver Jeremiah Smith broke program receptions and touchdown records with 11 catches for 206 yards and two scores in a 31-14 win over Iowa, while No. 7 Alabama's 56-23 rout of Mississippi State and No. 25 Missouri's 45-17 upset of No. 8 Florida were the weekend's signature results. Bleacher Report's post-Week 5 top 25 has Georgia, Texas, and Notre Dame at 1-2-3.

sports.detail: Fell to 3-1 (0-1 Big Ten) in a road loss at No. 18 USC on Saturday. Punter Hunter Green was named to the Ray Guy Award's "Ray's 8" for Week Five. Next: host No. 20 Iowa at Husky Stadium Oct. 9 — the Hawkeyes' first trip to Montlake in 63 years.

Added former Oregon assistant Mike Mennenga to the staff and brought in six transfers (Beasley, Comer, Friedrichsen, Venters, Watts, Zrno) to pair with returning starter Wesley Yates III. First look: an exhibition vs. rival Washington State Oct. 25 — the first-ever October meeting in the 110-year rivalry, with no regular-season game this year.

Beat the Chargers 30-23 Sunday to improve to 3-1, bouncing back from last week's loss to Washington. Sam Darnold threw for 168 yards and two touchdowns, and Emanuel Wilson scored both through the air and on the ground as Seattle handed L.A. its fourth straight loss.

Host Phoenix at Little Caesars Arena tonight (7 PM ET) in their preseason opener — first look at the roster since locking up Jalen Duren on a five-year, $200M extension. New faces include John Collins, Isaiah Joe, Taurean Prince, and No. 17 pick Ebuka Okorie.

GM Jerry Dipoto confirmed Seattle "will go outside to hire our manager," saying the club needs "fresh thought," after Torey Lovullo — seen as a leading candidate — re-signed with Arizona instead. Prior MLB managerial experience is "preferred" but not required for the club's third manager search since 2024.

DXY near an 18-month high (102.27) on French fiscal turmoil — watch EUR/GBP for further haven-flow spillover
Schneider Electric's $22B all-cash bid for PTC Corp — watch for competing bids or regulatory pushback

deepDive.title: Why a Weak Jobs Report Sent Yields to a 24-Year High
content: Today's brief contains a sequence that looks backwards at first glance: September payrolls came in at just 29,000 and unemployment ticked up to 4.2%, yet the 10-year Treasury yield spiked intraday to 5.349% — its highest level since April 2002 — before settling at 5.31%. Conventional wisdom says weak labor data should pull yields down, since it raises the odds the Fed eases policy. Instead, long-end yields rose while the 2-year, which tracks near-term Fed expectations most directly, actually eased to 4.82%. Understanding why those two things happened on the same day, in opposite directions, requires taking apart what a long-term bond yield is actually made of.

A 10-year yield isn't one number — it's the sum of the expected average path of short-term interest rates over the next decade plus a term premium, the extra compensation investors demand for the risk of locking up money for ten years instead of rolling over short-term bills. Soft jobs data mainly moves the first piece, nudging down the expected rate path and explaining the front end's modest rally. But the term premium is driven by a different set of worries entirely: inflation uncertainty, the government's financing needs, and global appetite for long-duration sovereign debt. Today, a fiscal shock in France was rattling European bond markets at the same time, and that kind of cross-border stress tends to raise the term premium demanded on all long-duration sovereign paper, U.S. Treasuries included, even as it ironically strengthens the dollar through relative safe-haven flows.

The historical parallel that makes this concrete is the 1994 "bond market massacre," when the 10-year yield rose roughly 200 basis points over the year even as the Fed was only modestly raising short rates — investors demanded a much larger term premium after years of underpricing inflation and fiscal risk, and bond portfolio losses that year were larger than in many down years for stocks. The lesson that generalizes: term premium can swing the long end of the curve by more than the policy-rate path does, which is exactly what's splitting the 2s/10s move today. Most casual market-watchers conflate "yields rose" with "the market expects higher rates," when it may really mean "investors want more compensation for existing risks," a materially different signal for credit markets and mortgage pricing alike.

For Chris, the practical takeaway is to watch the shape of the curve, not just the 10-year print in isolation — a steepening move (long yields up, short yields flat or down) like today's is a term-premium story, while a parallel shift across all maturities would signal the market repricing the Fed's whole policy path. This week's Fed minutes release will be the next real test: if officials' internal debate reads dovish while long yields stay elevated anyway, that's confirmation the term-premium channel, not rate expectations, is what's driving this move — and it's the same channel that determines whether this week's softer jobs data actually translates into cheaper mortgage and corporate borrowing costs, or gets offset entirely by investors simply demanding more yield to hold the paper.
